extracted.intended_audience: media sociologists, communication scholars, and public-relations practitioners interested in news sourcing and press-release strategy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for designing press releases to win media pickup by competing strategically against other sources; focused on timing, framing, coalitions, and tactical use of limited resources. Draws on Schlesinger's critique of the 'primary definers' model to offer practical heuristics for release-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic-competition awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: A release should be designed knowing that competing sources will issue counter-releases. Anticipate the most likely counter-frame and respond pre-emptively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan releases as moves in a contest, not as isolated communications. Map likely rival messages and craft pre-emptive text or evidence to blunt them; consider what counter-releases could be produced and prepare rebuttals or alternative framings in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition-building signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases that bring multiple distinct sources into alignment (cross-institution co-sign, multi-stakeholder endorsement) outperform releases from a single source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek co-signers or endorsements from diverse institutions or stakeholder types to signal broader legitimacy and increase chances of pickup; explicit multi-source packages are more attractive to journalists than lone-actor releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal-elite-division exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where elite institutions are divided (a regulator vs. an industry, two academic disciplines), a release that surfaces and uses the division gains traction even from a less-resourced position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and publicize splits within dominant institutions to create openings; framing that exposes intra-elite disagreement can make a less-resourced source appear more newsworthy and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing is a key strategic resource. Releases timed to compete for an editor's attention slot (after a competing release fails, before a competing release lands) earn disproportionate pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn editorial rhythms and deadlines; schedule release distribution to exploit attention gaps or to pre-empt competitor releases. Timing can substitute for resources if it aligns with journalists' availability and news cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource-substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: A release from a resource-poor source can substitute strategic intelligence for institutional resources: knowing the editor's deadline, the beat's current obsession, the rival source's vulnerabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge of journalists' needs and beats, and of rival weaknesses, to craft highly targeted, usable releases. Tactical intelligence (who, when, what matters now) can overcome lack of institutional clout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame contestability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejects the assumption that the dominant frame will automatically win. A release with a more usable frame for the journalist will displace a frame from a more-resourced source if the alternative is better made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make your frame operational and journalist-ready (clear problem, concise angle, workable lede). Emphasize usability for reporting—concrete hooks, clear implications, and accessible metaphors increase likelihood of adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat-network entry
rubrics_metrics.description: A release should target one beat at high quality before attempting cross-beat distribution; successful entry to one beat opens others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus distribution and tailoring on a single beat to build credibility and relationships; once established on one beat, leverage that track record to expand into adjacent beats instead of broad, unfocused circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability-trail
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases that generate accountability questions (who funded it, who vetted it) on the more-resourced rival earn the contest by shifting the journalist's burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tactics that prompt journalists to scrutinize rivals (raise questions about funding, vetting, methodology) so attention shifts away from your resource disadvantage. Framing that creates doubt about a dominant source can be an effective strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-run reputation building
rubrics_metrics.description: Pickup is partly a function of repeated honest dealings; one accurate release builds the credit balance that allows the next release to earn quick acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in consistent, accurate, and fair interactions with journalists over time. Short-term tactical gains help, but sustained credibility (honesty, reliability) accumulates 'credit' that increases future pickup probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter-rival source-package
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases competing against a major-institution release should bring a complete counter-package: counter-data, counter-expert, counter-narrative, counter-image. Partial counter-packages get filtered out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When contesting a powerful source, deliver a full alternative—evidence, authoritative spokespeople, coherent narrative, and visuals—so journalists can easily use it as a substitute; half-measures are likely to be ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-worthiness implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Pickup is not deterministically a function of issuer rank; less-resourced issuers can win contested news agenda by playing strategic competition well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate release pickup prospectus by strategic factors (timing, coalitions, usable frames, exploitation of elite divisions, completeness of package) rather than by issuer prestige alone. Use this principle to prioritize tactics that maximize contest-winning potential.
